title: Top Chef Alum Rasika Venkatesa Opens Mythily, Progressive South Indian Restaurant in Williamsburg
excerpt: Named for her Chennai grandmother, the 45-seat Mythily reworks Tamil home cooking with French Laundry technique — and a Kickstarter-funded build-out behind it.
body:
• Mythily, a progressive South Indian restaurant from Top Chef alum Rasika Venkatesa, has opened at 129 Havemeyer Street in Williamsburg, Brooklyn.
  • The 45-seat restaurant is named for the chef's grandmother, Mythily Ramachandran, and is built on the Tamil home cooking she grew up with in Chennai.
  • The menu reworks South Indian flavours in new forms — a Davangere-style benne dosa, scallop with puli inji, and a short rib with bone marrow kozhumbu among them.
  • Planning a visit: Mythily is open Wednesday to Saturday, 5pm to 10pm, and Sunday, 4pm to 9pm, with reservations through SevenRooms.

A new South Indian restaurant with an unusually personal backstory has opened in Williamsburg. Mythily, from chef Rasika Venkatesa, began serving at 129 Havemeyer Street on September 30, and Time Out coverage and New York food media have since picked it out as one of the season's notable openings. Time Out had already named Venkatesa one of its Best Young Chefs before the restaurant existed; Mythily is the brick-and-mortar debut that followed.

The restaurant takes its name from the chef's grandmother, Mythily Ramachandran, whose cooking in Chennai first taught her how food holds a family together. According to What Now New York's opening report, the 45-seat room is intended as a personal expression of her South Indian heritage, centred on Tamil Nadu but ranging across the wider region.

From the French Laundry to Havemeyer Street

Venkatesa's resume is not typical for a neighbourhood opening. Born and raised in Chennai, she began her professional career at Thomas Keller's three-Michelin-starred The French Laundry in California, then joined Mourad in San Francisco, rising to chef de cuisine by the age of 23 and being named a Rising Star Chef of San Francisco in 2022. She later competed on Season 21 of Top Chef, where cooking Indian food on the show became a turning point in finding her own voice, What Now reported.

The road to a restaurant of her own ran through New York pop-ups. After arriving in the city in 2024, she cooked a four-month residency, wine-bar pop-ups and private events under the Mythily name, building the menu in public before signing a lease with co-founders Varun Kandadi and Nicolas Chavotier. A community Kickstarter raised over $100,000 toward the build-out, and the team documented months of hands-on demolition before opening day, according to the Time Out account summarised by Briefly.

What is on the menu

The cooking applies fine-dining technique to flavours from home. We Heart's report lists small plates including green apple and fennel with charred cucumber, boondi, stracciatella and rasam, and a sweet, dry-cured scallop with puli inji, Concord grapes and a panakam granita. A benne dosa follows the style of Davangere, in Karnataka, served with seasonal masala and sambar.

Larger plates include a chicken ballotine in kozhi kozhumbu, tilefish with a Nagapattinam manga curry, slow-roasted cabbage, and the signature short rib — cured overnight, cooked for six hours, and served with plums, maitake mushrooms and bone marrow kozhumbu. Desserts pair ras malai with tres leches, and filter coffee appears as a soft serve with a peanut and jaggery brittle crumble. Drinks lean low-ABV and non-alcoholic, built on housemade cordials, ferments and spice-infused shochu, alongside Brooklyn beers and European wines.

The room

The design, by Venkatesa and Kandadi with Demir Purisic of Studio Purisic, takes its cues from a South Indian village, both opening reports note. Deep reds, greens and warm neutrals reference soil, forests and paddy fields, with Moroccan clay plaster, sapele wood and brass lighting. A semi-open kitchen in red limewash sits under a green ceiling, and a nine-seat bar is topped with Moulin Rouge quartzite. Artwork throughout returns to the restaurant's founding theme: grandmothers and grandchildren.

Why it matters for New York's Indian food scene

New York has no shortage of Indian restaurants, but regionally specific South Indian cooking presented at this level remains comparatively rare, and rarer still from a chef cooking her own family's food rather than a generic pan-Indian menu. Greenpointers marked the opening for its north Brooklyn readership on day one. For diaspora diners, the practical details are on the restaurant's site at mythily.nyc: dinner only, Wednesday to Sunday, at 129 Havemeyer Street, with reservations through SevenRooms — worth booking ahead while opening coverage is still drawing crowds.
